rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās takes “none of you but will come to it” as an address specifically to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال: في قول الله تعالى: { وإن منكم إلا واردها } قال: هذا خطاب للكفار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās read “wa-in minhum” (“none of them”), aligning the address with the preceding references to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: أنه كان يقرأ «وإن منهم» ردا على الآيات التي قبلها في الكفار

rows.speaker: عكرمة وجماعة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and a group also read “wa-in minhum”; al-Qurṭubī sees no objection to this reading.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قرأ عكرمة وجماعة وعليها فلا شغب في هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group construes “among you” as unbelievers addressed by the Prophet, an interpretation al-Qurṭubī calls readily intelligible.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: المراد ب«منكم» الكفرة والمعنى: قل لهم يا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, the second-person suffix can refer back to the third-person object in “We will gather them”; Arabic permits such shifts.
rows.anchor: فلا ينكر رجوع الكاف إلى الهاء فقد عرف ذلك

rows.speaker: الأكثر
rows.claim: Most commentators take the whole world as the addressee and hold that everyone must pass through the Fire, which is the source of disagreement over passage.
rows.anchor: وقال الأكثر: المخاطب العالم كله، ولا بد من ورود الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense of coming to the Fire is entry, since a hadith says it touches a person; believers find it cool and safe and escape unharmed.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الورود الدخول لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام: «فتمسه النار»

rows.speaker: خالد بن معدان
rows.claim: Khalid ibn Maʿdan says Paradise’s people will be told that they did come to the Fire but found it reduced to ashes.
rows.anchor: قال خالد بن معدان: إذا دخل أهل الجنة الجنة قالوا: ألم يقل ربنا: إنا نرد النار؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entry without harm reconciles the reports: one who comes to the Fire without suffering its blaze has in effect been kept far away and rescued.
rows.anchor: فإن من وردها ولم تؤذه بلهبها وحرها فقد أبعد عنها ونجي منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He will not categorically say prophets enter Hell; all creation comes to it, while sinners enter for their crimes and the blessed through intercession, a vast difference between the two entries.
rows.anchor: لا نطلق هذا، ولكن نقول: إن الخلق جميعا يردونها

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī defends the ʿUthmānic codex and common reading: Arabic may shift from third-person reference to direct address.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري محتجا لمصحف عثمان وقراءة العامة: جائز في اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example “this was your recompense” shifts from third-person reference to second-person address; al-Qurṭubī says the point was already discussed under Jonah.
rows.anchor: فأبدل الكاف من الهاء. وقد تقدم هذا المعنى في «يونس»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith’s exception “except the measure of an oath” may be disjunctive, meaning an oath must be discharged; passage can mean crossing the bridge, seeing the Fire, or safe entry, without being touched by it.
rows.anchor: الاستثناء في قوله عليه السلام: «إلا تحلة القسم» يحتمل أن يكون استثناء منقطعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Someone shielded from the Fire has not been touched by it; the report that three dead children become a shield supports this interpretation.
rows.anchor: ومن وقي النار وستر عنها فلن تمسه أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report about three children explains the preceding report because it mentions patient acceptance; Mālik placed it immediately after the first as its explanation.
rows.anchor: هذا الحديث يفسر الأول لأن فيه ذكر الحسبة ولذلك جعله مالك بأثره مفسرا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that three children who died before puberty become a shield or lead to Paradise restricts the other report: “not reaching sin” means not reaching puberty or moral responsibility.
rows.anchor: ومعناه عند أهل العلم لم يبلغوا الحلم ولم يبلغوا أن يلزمهم حنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim children who die before acquiring deeds are in Paradise; al-Qurṭubī calls this consensus, against an aberrant rejected Jabrī view that leaves them to God’s discretion.
rows.anchor: وهذا إجماع من العلماء في أن أطفال المسلمين في الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Children who die before acquiring deeds are among those destined for happiness in the womb, as hadith reports and consensus show.
rows.anchor: وأن من مات من أطفال المسلمين قبل الاكتساب فهو ممن سعد في بطن أمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report to ʿĀʾisha that God created people for Paradise or Hell while they were in their fathers’ loins is weak and rejected; transmitter Ṭalḥa ibn Yaḥyā is weak and the report stands alone.
rows.anchor: ساقط ضعيف مردود بالإجماع والآثار، وطلحة بن يحيى الذي يرويه ضعيف

rows.speaker: معاوية بن قرة عن أبيه
rows.claim: An Anṣārī whose young son died was told that the child would open whichever gate of Paradise he approached; the Prophet said this applied to Muslims generally.
rows.anchor: أن رجلا من الأنصار مات له ابن صغير فوجد عليه

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abū ʿUmar calls the Anṣārī-child report sound and authentic, consistent with majority consensus, and a rebuttal to Yaḥyā’s contrary report.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمر: هذا حديث ثابت صحيح بمعنى ما ذكرناه مع إجماع الجمهور

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abū ʿUmar says such glad tidings concern those who maintained obligations, avoided major sins, and patiently sought reward; the original audience were the Companions.
rows.anchor: والوجه عندي في هذا الحديث وما أشبهه من الآثار أنها لمن حافظ على أداء فرائضه

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh reports that some claimed 21:101 abrogated this verse, but al-Qurṭubī rejects abrogation: being unharmed by the Fire already means being kept away from it.
rows.anchor: وذكر النقاش عن بعضهم أنه قال: نسخ قوله تعالى: { وإن منكم إلا واردها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report depicts the Fire telling a believer to pass because the believer’s light has extinguished its flames.
rows.anchor: تقول النار للمؤمن يوم القيامة جز يا مؤمن فقد أطفأ نورك لهبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Inevitable decree” means an obligatory determination that God decreed for you; Ibn Masʿūd glosses it as a binding oath.
rows.anchor: الحتم إيجاب القضاء أي كان ذلك حتما. «مقضيا» أي قضاه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious are rescued and wrongdoers left crouching in Hell; the wording supports actual entry, since it does not say God will make them enter.
rows.anchor: وهذا مما يدل على أن الورود الدخول لأنه لم يقل: وندخل الظالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adopted doctrine is that a major sinner may enter Hell, be punished in proportion to the sin, and then be rescued.
rows.anchor: والمذهب أن صاحب الكبيرة وإن دخلها فإنه يعاقب بقدر ذنبه ثم ينجو

rows.speaker: المرجئة
rows.claim: The Murjiʾa say the major sinner does not enter Hell.
rows.anchor: وقالت المرجئة: لا يدخل

rows.speaker: الوعيدية
rows.claim: The Waʿīdiyya say the major sinner remains in Hell forever.
rows.anchor: وقالت الوعيدية: يخلد

rows.speaker: عاصم الجحدري ومعاوية بن قرة
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra read “nunajjī” with a light jīm, from “anjā”; Ḥamīd, Yaʿqūb, and al-Kisāʾī do too, while other readers double it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم الجحدري ومعاوية بن قرة «ثم ننجي» مخففة من أنجى

rows.speaker: ابن أبي ليلى
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Laylā reads “thammah” with open tāʾ, meaning “there”; its hāʾ may mark a vowel and disappear in liaison or mark feminine place and remain as tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي ليلى «ثمه» بفتح الثاء أي هناك. و«ثم» ظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people addressed are disbelievers already mentioned in 19:66 and 19:72; worldly status is their answer to Qurʾānic recitation.
rows.anchor: على الكفار الذين سبق ذكرهم في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They use wealth and stronger support as proof of religious truth to sow doubt among the vulnerable, overlooking poor unbelievers and rich Muslims; God keeps His friends from worldly delusion.
rows.anchor: وغرضهم إدخال الشبهة على المستضعفين وإيهامهم أن من كثر ماله دل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clear” may mean well-articulated words, concise meanings, and evident purposes; or ambiguous verses clarified by decisive ones or the Prophet’s words and deeds; or manifest inimitable signs and proofs.
rows.anchor: مرتلات الألفاظ، ملخصة المعاني، مبينات المقاصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī takes “clear” as an emphatic circumstantial description: God’s verses are necessarily lucid proofs, as 2:91 similarly calls the Book the truth.
rows.anchor: والوجه أن تكون حالا مؤكدة كقوله تعالى: وهو الحق مصدقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers are Quraysh polytheists, especially al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and companions; the believers are the Prophet’s poor Companions.
rows.anchor: يريد مشركي قريش النضر بن الحارث وأصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ rough appearance and worn clothes contrasted with the polytheists’ groomed hair, oiled heads, and fine clothes.
rows.anchor: وكانت فيهم قشافة، وفي عيشهم خشونة، وفي ثيابهم رثاثة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وابن محيصن وحميد وشبل بن عباد
rows.claim: These readers pronounce “maqāman” with ḍamma, meaning a residence or the verbal noun “residing.”
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وابن محيصن وحميد وشبل بن عباد «مقاما» بضم الميم

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The other readers pronounce it with fatḥa, meaning a home or place for conducting important affairs, hence greater prestige and supporters.
rows.anchor: الباقون «مقاما» بالفتح، أي منزلا ومسكنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains “nadī” as an assembly and also as outward appearance; lexically it is a meeting and conversation place.
rows.anchor: «وأحسن نديا» أي مجلسا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dar al-Nadwa was named for Quraysh’s council there; “nādāhu” means to sit with someone in the gathering. The cited line illustrating “unādī” appears in the next source segment.
rows.anchor: ومنه دار الندوة لأن المشركين كانوا يتشاورون فيها في أمورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line about calling the families of al-Walīd and Jaʿfar illustrates “unādī” in the sense of assembly or meeting.
rows.anchor: أنادي به آل الوليد وجعفرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qarn” means a nation or community; earlier generations had abundant possessions and “athāth” means household goods.
rows.anchor: أي من أمة وجماعة. { هم أحسن أثاثا } أي متاعا كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation distinguishes new furnishings, “athāth,” from used household goods, “kharathī”; a verse by al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Ṭūsī illustrates the latter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو ما جد من الفرش والخرثي ما لبس منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “athāth” as appearance and Muqātil as clothing.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هيئة. مقاتل: ثيابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Riya” means a fine appearance; five readings are listed, including Medinan unhamzated, Kufan hamzated, Ṭalḥa’s softened form, Ibn ʿAbbās’s zāy form, and an alternative hamzated form.
rows.anchor: وفيه خمس قراءات: قرأ أهل المدينة «وريا» بغير همز

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: Their unhamzated reading may derive from “raʾaytu,” with hamza softened into yāʾ and the yāʾs merged, fitting the rhyme and meaning good appearance and clothing.
rows.anchor: أن تكون من رأيت ثم خففت الهمزة فأبدل منها ياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “al-raʾy” as appearance, yielding the sense that they had finer furnishings and clothing.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: الرئي المنظر فالمعنى: هم أحسن أثاثا ولباسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation of the unhamzated form derives it from well-watered skin from worldly blessing.
rows.anchor: أن جلودهم مرتوية من النعمة

rows.speaker: ورش عن نافع وابن ذكوان عن ابن عامر
rows.claim: These transmitters read “warʾiyyan” with hamza, as do the Kufans and Abū ʿAmr, following the original form from “raʾaytu.”
rows.anchor: وفي رواية ورش عن نافع وابن ذكوان عن ابن عامر «ورئيا» بالهمز

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif reads the word with one softened yāʾ; al-Qurṭubī suspects this is an error.
rows.anchor: وقراءة طلحة بن مصرف «وريا» بياء واحدة مخففة أحسبها غلطا

rows.speaker: بعض النحويين
rows.claim: Some grammarians derive the form from an original hamza changed to yāʾ, then delete one of the two yāʾs.
rows.anchor: وقد زعم بعض النحويين أنه كان أصلها الهمز فقلبت الهمزة ياء

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī proposes “riʾan” becoming “riyyan,” followed by transfer of the hamza’s vowel and its deletion.
rows.anchor: المهدوي: ويجوز أن يكون «ريئا» فقلبت ياء فصارت رييا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading uses metathesis to produce “riya”; Sibawayh records “rāʾ” as a form meaning “he saw.”
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ بعضهم «وريا» على القلب وهي القراءة الخامسة

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawharī says the hamzated form means visible beauty and conspicuous dress; Abū ʿUbayda cites a line by Muḥammad ibn Numayr al-Thaqafī as evidence.
rows.anchor: من همزه جعله من المنظر من رأيت، وهو ما رأته العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unhamzated reading may reflect hamza-softening or derive from healthy coloring; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and others read “ziyan,” meaning good bearing or beauty.
rows.anchor: ومن لم يهمز إما أن يكون على تخفيف الهمزة أو يكون من رويت ألوانهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبي بن كعب وسعيد بن جبير والأعسم المكي ويزيد البربري
rows.claim: These authorities read “ziyan” with zāy, meaning bearing and beauty; it may derive from “zawaytu,” gathered, with wāw changed to yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عباس وأبي بن كعب وسعيد بن جبير والأعسم المكي ويزيد البربري «وزيا» بالزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s expression “the earth was gathered for me” illustrates the root meaning “gathered.”
rows.anchor: " زويت لي الأرض " أي جمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The former peoples’ fine possessions did not avert death or God’s punishment, whether through later punishment or punishment in this life.
rows.anchor: أي فلم يغن ذلك عنهم شيئا من عذاب الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative “let the Merciful extend him” is an indicative threat: whoever persists in misguidance is left in ignorant excess, lengthening delusion and punishment.
rows.anchor: فلفظه لفظ الأمر ومعناه الخبر أي من كان في الضلالة مده الرحمن مدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the phrase as a prayer the Prophet is instructed to make against a wrongdoer, like wishing a thief’s hand be cut off; on this reading it answers the condition rather than reporting an event.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا دعاء أمر به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم تقول: من سرق مالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat resembles 3:178, where respite increases wrongdoing, and 6:110, where people are left wandering in transgression.
rows.anchor: نظيره: إنما نملي لهم ليزدادوا إثما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Man” can refer to one or many; “idhā” with a past-tense verb can refer to the future.
rows.anchor: لأن لفظ «من» يصلح للواحد والجمع. و«إذا» مع الماضي بمعنى المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised punishment may be defeat by believers through the sword and captivity, or the coming of the Hour and the Fire.
rows.anchor: والعذاب هنا إما أن يكون بنصر المؤمنين عليهم فيعذبونهم بالسيف والأسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When truth is disclosed they will know who has the worse abode and weaker forces; this answers the boast in 19:73 about the better residence and gathering.
rows.anchor: وهذا رد لقولهم: «أي الفريقين خير مقاما وأحسن نديا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God confirms believers in guidance, increases their support, and sends signs that deepen certainty as recompense.
rows.anchor: أي ويثبت الله المؤمنين على الهدى، ويزيدهم في النصرة

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil explain increased guidance as believers affirming abrogating and abrogated revelations, unlike those who reject them.
rows.anchor: قال معناه الكلبي ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further possible sense is that people guided to obedience are guided to Paradise; al-Qurṭubī says the interpretations are close.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل ثالثا: أي «ويزيد الله الذين اهتدوا» إلى الطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Growth in deeds, faith, and guidance has been discussed under Āl ʿImrān and elsewhere; the lasting good deeds were discussed under al-Kahf.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم القول في معنى زيادة الأعمال وزيادة الإيمان والهدى في «آل عمران»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lasting good deeds are better in reward and final return than the worldly possessions about which unbelievers boast.
rows.anchor: أي جزاء: { وخير مردا } أي في الآخرة مما افتخر به الكفار في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mard” can mean a better recompense to the doer; alternatively, a better destination where each person returns to his deeds.
rows.anchor: و«المرد» مصدر كالرد أي وخير ردا على عاملها بالثواب

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: Khabbāb had a debt owed by al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; when pressed to deny Muḥammad, he refused until the debtor died and was raised, and al-ʿĀṣ mocked that he would repay when restored to wealth and children. The report is transmitted by Muslim and Bukhārī.
rows.anchor: عن خباب قال كان لي على العاص بن وائل دين فأتيته أتقاضاه

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil say blacksmith Khabbāb had made jewelry for al-ʿĀṣ; al-ʿĀṣ mocked repayment in Paradise, claiming he would have wealth there and Khabbāb no greater entitlement.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي ومقاتل: كان خباب قينا فصاغ للعاص حليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boast about being granted wealth and children concerns al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, named in the reports.
rows.anchor: يعني العاص بن وائل الآيات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses looking into the unseen as looking into the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أنظر في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes it as knowing the unseen, including whether he will be in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: أعلم الغيب حتى يعلم أفي الجنة هو أم لا

rows.speaker: قتادة والثوري
rows.claim: Qatāda and al-Thawrī explain the covenant as a righteous deed; other views are monotheism, a promise, or al-Kalbī’s claim that he covenanted to enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة والثوري: أي عملا صالحا. وقيل: هو التوحيد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the verses were revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, but al-Qurṭubī prefers the al-ʿĀṣ report because it is recorded in the sound collections.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إن الآيات نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة. والأول أصح

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read “waladan” with ḍamma, while others use fatḥa; they may be dialect synonyms, though Qays uses the ḍamma form as plural and the fatḥa as singular.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي «وولدا» بضم الواو، والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: الحارث بن حلزة
rows.claim: A line by al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza uses the fatḥa form “waladan” to illustrate the word.
rows.anchor: ولقد رأيت معاشرا قد ثمروا مالا وولدا

rows.speaker: قيس
rows.claim: Qays treats the ḍamma form as plural and the fatḥa form as singular.
rows.anchor: أن قيسا تجعل الولد بالضم جمعا والولد بالفتح واحدا

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Māwardī lists a Paradise boast mocking God’s promise, or a claim to worldly wealth either from remaining in ancestral religion or as proof of religious truth.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله تعالى: { لأوتين مالا وولدا } وجهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says al-Kalbī’s Paradise reading best fits the hadiths, especially their explicit wording.
rows.anchor: قول الكلبي أشبه بظاهر الأحاديث، بل نصها يدل على ذلك

rows.speaker: مسروق
rows.claim: Masrūq heard Khabbāb report that al-ʿĀṣ expected wealth and children in the afterlife and promised repayment; al-Tirmidhī graded the report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: قال الترمذي: هذا حديث حسن صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening alif is interrogative because “am” follows; it arose from two alifs, with the second, hamzat al-waṣl, deleted.
rows.anchor: ألفه ألف استفهام لمجيء «أم» بعدها، ومعناه التوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike forms such as “a-llāhu” and “a-al-dhakrayn,” this question needs no lengthening to distinguish it from a statement: the interrogative has fatḥa and declarative kasra.
rows.anchor: ولم يحتاجوا إلى هذه المدة في قوله: «أطلع» لأن ألف الاستفهام مفتوحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kallā” has two senses, “indeed” or “no”; if “no,” one may pause on it, while “indeed” permits pausing before and restarting with it.
rows.anchor: وهو يكون بمعنيين: أحدهما: بمعنى حقا. والثاني: بمعنى لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kallā” does not occur in the first half of the Qurʾān but appears in the second; the correct pause depends on its meaning.
rows.anchor: ليس في النصف الأول ذكر «كلا» وإنما جاء ذكره في النصف الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One may pause at “ʿahdan” and begin “kallā” as “indeed, We will record what he says.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تقف على قوله: «عهدا» وتبتدىء «كلا» أي حقا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats “kallā” as a connective like “sawfa,” or as a self-sufficient rebuttal like yes or no; when it links to what follows in an oath, one should not pause on it.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: «كلا» بمنزلة سوف لأنها صلة، وهي حرف رد

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر محمد بن سعدان
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar ibn Saʿdān takes the same position on “kallā” as al-Farrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو جعفر محمد بن سعدان يقول في «كلا» مثل قول الفراء

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash defines “kallā” as rebuke and restraint.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: معنى كلا الردع والزجر

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī reports Abū al-ʿAbbās’s view that one should never stop at “kallā,” since its point comes afterward.
rows.anchor: لا يوقف على «كلا» في جميع القرآن لأنها جواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says the first interpretation is the exegetes’ position.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول هو قول أهل التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God preserves the man’s statement to recompense him and extends his punishment with additional torment.
rows.anchor: أي سنحفظ عليه قوله فنجازيه به في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We inherit what he says” can mean stripping him of worldly wealth and children; Ibn ʿAbbās and others say God inherits them after destroying him.
rows.anchor: أي نسلبه ما أعطيناه في الدنيا من مال وولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is that he is denied the afterlife wealth and children he desired, which are given instead to other Muslims.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نحرمه ما تمناه في الآخرة من مال وولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He comes alone, without wealth, children, or clan to defend him.
rows.anchor: أي منفردا لا مال له ولا ولد ولا عشيرة تنصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh polytheists took gods hoping for helpers and protection; “ʿizzan” may mean support, strength, or offspring, and is singular as an abstract noun.
rows.anchor: يعني مشركي قريش. و«عزا» معناه أعوانا ومنعة يعني أولادا

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawī notes that “ʿizz” can also mean abundant, heavy rain.
rows.anchor: والعز المطر الجود أيضا قاله الهروي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “ʿIzz” may refer directly to the gods or mean honor sought through them and protection from God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الكلام أن «عزا» راجع إلى الآلهة التي عبدوها من دون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gods will deny the worship, or idols will disclaim their worshippers as in 28:63; lifeless images cannot know they were worshipped.
rows.anchor: أو تجحد الآلهة عبادة المشركين لها كما قال

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the gods become enemies of their worshippers.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد والضحاك: يكونون لهم أعداء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the gods become a trial against worshippers: given speech, they ask God to punish those who worshipped them.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد: يكونون عليهم بلاء فتحشر آلهتهم

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī says “kallā” may rebuke and call attention to the previous claim or confirm what follows; its meaning controls pausing.
rows.anchor: «كلا» ردع وزجر وتنبيه ورد لكلام متقدم

rows.speaker: أبو نهيك
rows.claim: Abū Nuhayk reads “kallā” with tanwīn, with reports of both fatḥa and ḍamma on kāf; it can be an implied accusative verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو نهيك: «كلا سيكفرون» بالتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī gives four uses of “kallā”: confirmation, negation, attention, and an oath connective; only confirmation allows a pause.
rows.anchor: فتحصل في «كلا» أربعة معان: التحقيق وهو أن تكون بمعنى حقا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says “lā” only negates while “kallā” negates one thing and confirms another, illustrated by rejecting dates and affirming honey.
rows.anchor: «لا» تنفي فحسب، و«كلا» تنفي شيئا وتثبت شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ḍidd” can be singular or plural like “enemy” or “messenger,” or an abstract noun meaning help, matching “ʿizz” in the prior phrase.
rows.anchor: والضد يكون واحدا ويكون جمعا، كالعدو والرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage may concern idol worshippers or those who worshipped the Messiah, angels, jinn, or devils.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فيمن عبد المسيح أو الملائكة أو الجن أو الشياطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God empowered devils to mislead unbelievers, fulfilling the order to Iblīs in 17:64; another lexical sense is releasing them without protecting people, and al-Zajjāj says God assigned them to unbelievers.
rows.anchor: أي سلطناهم عليهم بالإغواء، وذلك حين قال لإبليس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “tuzzuhum” as agitating people from obedience toward sin, and also as inciting them to evil.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: تزعجهم إزعاجا من الطاعة إلى المعصية

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the devils lead unbelievers astray.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: تغويهم إغواء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains the verb as urging or driving them on; its root evokes motion and boiling.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: تشليهم إشلاء، وأصله الحركة والغليان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The core sense is agitation and incitement to sin; al-Jawharī also records mixing or joining as a separate lexical sense.
rows.anchor: والأز التهييج والإغراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes the Prophet praying while his chest sounded like a boiling cauldron from weeping.
rows.anchor: ولجوفه أزيز كأزيز المرجل من البكاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not hasten against them” means do not seek that their punishment be brought sooner.
rows.anchor: أي تطلب العذاب لهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says God counts their lifespans—days, nights, months, and years—until the punishment’s term ends.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: آجالهم يعني الأيام والليالي والشهور والسنين

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn ʿAbbās explain the count as breaths; Ibn ʿAbbās says breaths are counted as years are.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الأنفاس. ابن عباس: أي نعد أنفاسهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported objects are steps, pleasures, glances, moments, hours, or deeds, the latter attributed to Quṭrub.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخطوات. وقيل: اللذات. وقيل: اللحظات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God delays them so their sins increase; Ibn al-Sammāk warned al-Maʾmūn that numbered breaths with no replenishment soon run out.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا تعجل عليهم فإنما نؤخرهم ليزدادوا إثما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem says every passing breath removes part of one’s life and what sustains a person also brings death night after night.
rows.anchor: أنفاس تعد فكلما مضى نفس منك انتقصت به جزءا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report estimates 24,000 breaths each day and night, 12,000 in each; every breath is counted and the supply is not replenished.
rows.anchor: ويقال: إن أنفاس ابن آدم بين اليوم والليلة أربعة وعشرون ألف نفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits “Paradise”: the pious are gathered to the Garden and abode of honor belonging to the Merciful, as in 37:99.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف، أي إلى جنة الرحمن، ودار كرامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wafd” names arriving delegates, including those who go to a ruler as messengers in an important matter; it can also describe mounted delegations.
rows.anchor: والوفد اسم للوافدين، كما يقال: صوم وفطر وزور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mounted on steeds of their obedience” fits the usual custom of delegations arriving mounted; “wafd” is singular in form as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وفدا» أي ركبانا على نجائب طاعتهم

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the pious arrive mounted on camels.
rows.anchor: ابن جريج: وفدا على النجائب

rows.speaker: عمرو بن قيس الملائي
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn Qays al-Mullāʾī describes a believer’s fragrant righteous deed carrying him, while an unbeliever’s foul deed becomes his mount; Ibn al-ʿArabī says the chain is unsound.
rows.anchor: وقال عمرو بن قيس الملائي: إن المؤمن إذا خرج من قبره استقبله عمله

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī also transmits the deeds-as-mounts report from Ibn ʿAbbās and says people receive the kind of jeweled horse, camel, or ship they loved.
rows.anchor: وذكر هذا الخبر في تفسيره أبو نصر عبد الرحيم بن عبد الكريم القشيري

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī asks how God’s delegation will be mounted since kings’ delegations ride; the question continues in the next segment’s report.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا عن علي رضي الله عنه: ولما نزلت الآية

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: The Prophet says angels meet believers returning from standing before God on white Paradise she-camels, give them fine robes, and carry them to Paradise, where angels greet them (39:73).
rows.anchor: تلقت الملائكة المؤمنين بنوق بيض رحالها وأزمتها الذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports describe mounts and clothes only after the Judgment gathering; people first leave their graves barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised, though both conditions may occur in sequence.
rows.anchor: وهذا الخبر ينص على أنهم لا يركبون ولا يلبسون إلا من الموقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report of being raised barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās by al-Bukhārī and Muslim; a similar report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Unays was cited under Āl ʿImrān.
rows.anchor: بدليل حديث ابن عباس قال: قام فينا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بموعظة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra says the pious arrive as delegates mounted on camels.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو هريرة: «وفدا» على الإبل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes them riding Paradise camels with golden litters and jeweled saddles and reins.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: ركبانا يؤتون بنوق من الجنة عليها رحائل من الذهب

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī says they will not be gathered on foot but on mounts with golden or jeweled fittings that travel or fly at their command.
rows.anchor: وقال علي: ما يحشرون والله على أرجلهم، ولكن على نوق رحالها من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says each arrives on a favored camel, horse, or ship; “wafd” may also evoke delegates bringing glad tidings and expecting gifts, as the pious await reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما قال «وفدا» لأن من شأن الوفود عند العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Criminals are driven toward Hell thirsty, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, and al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: «وردا» عطاشا قاله ابن عباس وأبو هريرة رضي الله عنهما والحسن

rows.speaker: الأخفش والفراء وابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash, al-Farrāʾ, and Ibn al-Aʿrābī gloss “wirdan” as barefoot and walking; another view says individually.
rows.anchor: والأخفش والفراء وابن الأعرابي: حفاة مشاة

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī explains “wirdan” as people walking barefoot and thirsty like camels coming to water.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري: أي مشاة عطاشا، كالإبل ترد الماء

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī says “wirdan” signals thirst because animals generally come to water when thirsty.
rows.anchor: قوله: «وردا» يدل على العطش لأن الماء إنما يورد في الغالب للعطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The views are compatible: criminals are thirsty, barefoot, walking, and separate; alternatively “wirdan” is a verbal noun meaning they are driven to enter Hell.
rows.anchor: ولا تناقض بين هذه الأقوال، فيساقون عطاشا حفاة مشاة أفرادا

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArafa defines “wird” as those coming to water; the word can mean a thirsty group, animals arriving, water itself, a Qurʾānic portion, or fever day.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عرفة: الورد القوم يردون الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line describes people coming to a cistern, illustrating “al-ward” as water-seekers.
rows.anchor: يطمو إذا الورد عليه التكا أي الوراد الذين يريدون الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one reading, unbelievers cannot intercede, but believers who hold God’s covenant may; this is a disconnected exception with “man” in the accusative.
rows.anchor: أي هؤلاء الكفار لا يملكون الشفاعة لأحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “man” is nominative as substitute for the subject of “they possess”; on this connected exception, only a covenant-holder owns intercession.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو في موضع رفع على البدل من الواو في «يملكون»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Criminals” includes unbelievers and sinful believers; the latter may receive intercession, supported by a Muslim report of the Prophet seeking to intercede for those who testified to the two testimonies.
rows.anchor: و«المجرمين» في قوله: { ونسوق المجرمين إلى جهنم وردا } يعم الكفرة والعصاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports affirm that virtuous, learned, and righteous people intercede and are granted intercession.
rows.anchor: وتظاهرت الأخبار بأن أهل الفضل والعلم والصلاح يشفعون فيشفعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first interpretation, idolaters’ intercession for anyone and idols’ intercession for their worshippers will fail, as in 74:48.
rows.anchor: فلا تقبل غدا شفاعة عبدة الأصنام لأحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading permits intercession only by God’s permission, as in 2:255; the covenant comprehensively means faith and deeds qualifying a person to intercede.
rows.anchor: أي إذا أذن له الله في الشفاعة. كما قال: من ذا الذي يشفع عنده إلا بإذنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines the covenant as the testimony that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: العهد لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: مقاتل وابن عباس
rows.claim: Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās say only someone who testifies to God’s oneness, disavows independent power, and hopes only in God can intercede.
rows.anchor: لا يشفع إلا من شهد أن لا إله إلا الله، وتبرأ من الحول والقوة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports a morning and evening covenant prayer: the worshipper testifies to God’s oneness and Muḥammad’s messengerhood, entrusts himself to God’s mercy, and asks for a covenant fulfilled on Judgment Day; a caller then summons its holders to Paradise.
rows.anchor: أيعجز أحدكم أن يتخذ كل صباح ومساء عند الله عهدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming the Merciful has taken a child include Jews, Christians, and those who call the angels God’s daughters.
rows.anchor: يعني اليهود والنصارى، ومن زعم أن الملائكة بنات الله

rows.speaker: يحيى والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وعاصم وخلف
rows.claim: These readers use “walad” with ḍamma and still lām in four locations; others use fatḥa throughout, and both forms are dialect variants.
rows.anchor: قرأ يحيى والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وعاصم وخلف: «ولدا» بضم الواو

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ومجاهد وحميد وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: These authorities join the ḍamma reading specifically in Sūrat Nūḥ.
rows.anchor: ووافقهم في «نوح» خاصة ابن كثير ومجاهد وحميد وأبو عمرو ويعقوب

rows.speaker: قيس
rows.claim: Qays uses the ḍamma form as plural and fatḥa as singular; other grammarians allow either form as singular or plural, or treat them as variants.
rows.anchor: وقيس يجعلون الولد بالضم جمعا والولد بالفتح واحدا

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās rejects Abū ʿUbayd’s claim that “walad” is used for either parent’s children while “wild” is restricted to one side; linguists do not recognize that distinction.
rows.anchor: وفرق أبو عبيد بينهما فزعم أن الولد يكون للأهل والولد جميعا

rows.speaker: محمد بن الوليد
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd allows “walad” as plural on patterns such as “wuthan” and “asad,” or as a synonym for the other form.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون ولد جمع ولد، كما يقال وثن ووثن وأسد وأسد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وغيرهما
rows.claim: They gloss “an enormous thing” as something dreadful and immense.
rows.anchor: أي منكرا عظيما عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وغيرهما

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawharī explains “idd” as a calamity or terrible matter, with related forms for affliction and severity.
rows.anchor: الإد والإدة الداهية والأمر الفظيع

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī reads “iddan” with fatḥa; al-Naḥḥās explains it as bringing a tremendously objectionable thing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي «أدا» بفتح الهمزة

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī records three forms: the common kasra, al-Sulamī’s fatḥa, and “ādd,” attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-ʿĀliya and associated with a heavy burden.
rows.anchor: وفيه ثلاث لغات «إدا» بالكسر وهي قراءة العامة

rows.speaker: نافع ويحيى والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers use masculine “yakādu” because the verb precedes its subject; the common reading is feminine here and in al-Shūrā.
rows.anchor: وقراءة نافع ويحيى والكسائي «يكاد» بالياء لتقدم الفعل

rows.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وحفص وغيرهم
rows.claim: These readers use the doubled-tāʾ form “tafaṭṭarna”; Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir agree in al-Shūrā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير وحفص وغيرهم بتاء بعد الياء وشد الطاء من التفطر

rows.speaker: حمزة وابن عامر وأبو عمرو وأبو بكر والمفضل
rows.claim: Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir here, and Abū ʿAmr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal in both passages, read “yanfaṭirna”; Abū ʿUbayd prefers it by comparison with 82:1 and 73:18.
rows.anchor: وقرأا هنا «ينفطرن» من الانفطار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth splitting means it cracks apart; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the mountains’ fall as a demolition with a loud sound.
rows.anchor: وقوله: { وتنشق الأرض } أي تتصدع

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar transmits that “hadd” means demolition and “haddah” collapse; other lexicographers define it as violent collapse or something that breaks one’s strength.
rows.anchor: قال شمر: قال أحمد بن غياث المروزي: الهد الهدم والهدة

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says “hadd” may describe a weak man, as in “I am no weakling.”
rows.anchor: والهد الرجل الضعيف يقول الرجل للرجل إذا أوعده

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī defines “hadd” with fatḥa as a generous, noble man, and cites poetry contrasting brave people with weaklings.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: الهد من الرجال الجواد الكريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Haddah” is the crash of a wall; “hād” is a deep sound heard by coastal people from the sea, sometimes accompanying an earthquake.
rows.anchor: والهدة صوت وقع الحائط ونحوه

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās treats “haddan” as a verbal noun because “takhirr” means to fall with a crash; another view makes it a circumstantial description, “collapsed.”
rows.anchor: «هدا» مصدر لأن معنى «تخر» تهد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ parses “an” in “because they claimed” as accusative after dropping a preposition; al-Kisāʾī reportedly assigns genitive under an understood preposition.
rows.anchor: «أن» في موضع نصب عند الفراء بمعنى لأن دعوا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says a mountain asks another whether anyone remembered God that day and rejoices if told yes; he asks whether mountains hear false speech but not good speech.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن مسعود: إن الجبل ليقول للجبل

rows.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
rows.claim: A Syrian report says earth and trees benefited people until sinful humans claimed the Merciful had a child, after which earth shuddered and trees grew thorns.
rows.anchor: قال: إن الله تعالى لما خلق الأرض وخلق ما فيها من الشجر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says mountains, trees, seas, and fish bristled in distress, with thorns appearing in plants and fish.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: اقشعرت الجبال وما فيها من الأشجار، والبحار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وكعب
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Kaʿb say creation except humans and jinn trembled and nearly collapsed; angels grew angry, Hell blazed, and earth and vegetation were changed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا وكعب: فزعت السموات والأرض والجبال

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says God’s enemies nearly brought the Hour upon themselves through this immense claim.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب: لقد كاد أعداء الله أن يقيموا علينا الساعة

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī agrees this is a tremendous utterance; disbelief cannot diminish God’s kingdom and faith cannot increase it, so He permits the blasphemers’ words without being harmed.
rows.anchor: ولولا أن الباري تبارك وتعالى لا يضعه كفر الكافر، ولا يرفعه إيمان المؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A child entails shared kind and origination from a parent who has an origin; this is impossible and unfit for God, as discussed under al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: لأن الولد يقتضي الجنسية والحدوث على ما بيناه في «البقرة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line describes something inaccessible even to a level plain or mountain, illustrating “should be.”
rows.anchor: ما ينبغي دونها سهل ولا جبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In” is negative: everyone in heaven and earth will come on Judgment Day acknowledging God’s lordship in submission, as in 27:87; all are His servants, so none can be His child.
rows.anchor: أي ما كل من في السموات والأرض إلا وهو يأتي يوم القيامة مقرا له بالعبودية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ātī” is written with yāʾ; its original tanwīn is dropped for ease and the form is annexed.
rows.anchor: و«آتي» بالياء في الخط، والأصل التنوين فحذف استخفافا وأضيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse proves a parent cannot own a child: God contrasts sonship with servitude, which cannot coexist; if a father cannot own his son, the son cannot own his father all the more.
rows.anchor: وقد أبان الله تعالى المنافاة بين الأولاد والملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound Muslim report says a child cannot repay a parent except by finding the parent enslaved, buying him, and freeing him.
rows.anchor: لا يجزي ولد والدا إلا أن يجده مملوكا فيشتريه فيعتقه

rows.speaker: إسحاق بن راهويه
rows.claim: Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh interprets emancipation of a share in a slave as referring only to male slaves, so freeing a share in a female would not complete emancipation.
rows.anchor: ذهب إسحاق بن راهويه في تأويل قوله عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reject Isḥāq’s distinction and include male and female slaves, since “ʿabd” is generic and this verse encompasses both.
rows.anchor: وهو على خلاف ما ذهب إليه الجمهور من السلف ومن بعدهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A divine saying transmitted by al-Bukhārī through Abū Hurayra says Adam’s son falsely denies resurrection and insults God by claiming He has a child, though He is One and has no offspring or equal.
rows.anchor: كذبني ابن آدم ولم يكن له ذلك وشتمني ولم يكن له ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion had appeared under al-Baqara and elsewhere; repeating it here is appropriate.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم في «البقرة» وغيرها وإعادته في مثل هذا الموضع حسن جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the number of everyone; the repeated counting reinforces that none is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: أي علم عددهم { وعدهم عدا } تأكيد أي فلا يخفى عليه أحد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says al-Muḥṣī is among God’s names in Abū Hurayra’s report in al-Tirmidhī; the verb’s derivation supports it.
rows.anchor: ووقع لنا في أسمائه سبحانه المحصي أعني في السنة من حديث أبي هريرة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الإسفرايني
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī explains al-Muḥṣī as never distracted by multitude from knowing each motion and falling leaf, since He creates them; he cites 67:14.
rows.anchor: ومنها المحصي ويختص بأنه لا تشغله الكثرة عن العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the counting as people’s acknowledgment of servitude and testimony to God’s lordship.
rows.anchor: ووقع في تفسير ابن عباس أن معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone comes alone, without defender or useful wealth; only deeds benefit, as in 26:88–89, where neither wealth nor children avail except a sound heart.
rows.anchor: أي واحدا لا ناصر له ولا مال معه ينفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular verb follows the form of “kull,” while the plural follows its meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال: { وكلهم آتيه } على لفظ كل وعلى المعنى آتوه

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī argues that people reject enslaving their children, yet all are God’s servants, so they should not claim for God what they reject for themselves.
rows.anchor: وفيه إشارة إلى أنكم لا ترضون لأنفسكم باستعباد أولادكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their double standard also appears when they dislike daughters for themselves yet call angels or idols God’s daughters; 6:136 illustrates their unequal allocation.
rows.anchor: فما كان لشركآئهم فلا يصل إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God clarified the Qurʾān in the Prophet’s Arabic tongue and made it easy for those who reflect; alternatively, it was revealed in Arabic so its audience could readily understand it.
rows.anchor: يعني بيناه بلسانك العربي وجعلناه سهلا على من تدبره وتأمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings are for believers; “ludd” is the plural of “aladd,” fiercely disputatious, as in 2:204, and a cited poem illustrates it.
rows.anchor: اللُد جمع الألد وهو الشديد الخصومة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda defines the disputatious person as one who rejects truth and asserts falsehood.
rows.anchor: الألد الذي لا يقبل الحق ويدعي الباطل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says “ludd” are people deaf to truth.
rows.anchor: الحسن: اللد الصم عن الحق

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ describes them as the ears of the heart being deaf.
rows.anchor: قال الربيع: صم آذان القلوب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses the group as wicked people.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: فجارا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says they argue falsely.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: مجادلين في الباطل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls them fierce in argument.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: شدادا في الخصومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is unjust people who refuse to act rightly; the meanings are close and this group is singled out because less stubborn people are easier to guide.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الظالم الذي لا يستقيم والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destroyed “generation” means a nation or community; the warning is directed to Mecca’s inhabitants.
rows.anchor: أي من أمة وجماعة من الناس يخوف أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do you sense any of them?” means whether one sees or finds anyone; “rikz” may mean a voice, according to Ibn ʿAbbās and others, showing they died and were left with their deeds.
rows.anchor: في موضع نصب أي هل ترى منهم أحدا وتجد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd offers “ḥissan” as an explanation of the sound one might hear.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حسا قاله ابن زيد

rows.speaker: اليزيدي وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Yazīdī and Abū ʿUbayda say “rikz” is an indistinct sound or movement, like a troop’s murmur, and cite Labīd.
rows.anchor: الركز ما لا يفهم من صوت أو حركة قاله اليزيدي وأبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rikz” can mean a faint sound; related “rakaza” means burying a spear point in the earth, and lines by Ṭarafa and Dhū al-Rumma describe keenly detected hidden sounds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الصوت الخفي. ومنه ركز الرمح إذا غيب طرفه في الأرض
